title: Microsoft 365 Copilot rollout readiness checklist
summary: A gated checklist covering licensing, identity, data, security, support and communication that you can walk through before enabling Microsoft 365 Copilot for any user group.
body:
# Microsoft 365 Copilot rollout readiness checklist

Use this checklist as a go/no-go gate before each rollout wave. Each section has an owner, a pass criterion and the evidence you should keep. A wave can start only when every "Must" item is green; "Should" items can carry an agreed deadline.

## How to use it
1. Copy the checklist into a tracker (list, Planner, spreadsheet) with columns: Item, Owner, Status (Red/Amber/Green), Evidence link, Date.
2. Review it in a 45-minute readiness meeting with IT, security, data protection, HR/works council if applicable, and the business sponsor.
3. Re-run the data and security sections before every new wave, because content and permissions change.

## 1. Business case and scope (Must)
- A named executive sponsor and a named product owner exist.
- Three to five target scenarios are written down (for example meeting recaps, customer email drafts, report summaries) with a baseline time per task.
- Success metrics and a decision date are agreed before the pilot starts (see the pilot scorecard).
- Wave plan lists user groups, headcount and start dates.

## 2. Licensing and tenant prerequisites (Must)
- Eligible base licenses are in place for every planned user (check current requirements on Microsoft Learn, they change).
- Copilot licenses are purchased and assigned through a group so that removal is easy.
- Microsoft 365 Apps are on a supported update channel; Outlook, Teams and OneDrive clients are current.
- Teams meeting transcription and recording policies are decided, because recaps depend on them.
- Network and proxy rules allow the required Microsoft 365 endpoints.

## 3. Identity and access (Must)
- MFA is enforced for all pilot users; admins use phishing-resistant methods.
- Conditional Access applies to Copilot-relevant workloads; guest access rules are reviewed.
- No orphaned or shared accounts are in the pilot group.
- Privileged roles for Copilot administration are assigned just in time.

## 4. Data readiness (Must)
- Top 50 sites by content volume and top 50 by sensitivity are identified.
- Oversharing scan done: sites shared with Everyone or "Everyone except external users", broad groups, Anyone links (see the oversharing runbook).
- Sensitivity labels exist and are published; default labeling or auto-labeling covers at least the highest-risk content types.
- Retention policy for Copilot interactions is decided with compliance.
- Decision recorded on temporary guardrails (for example Restricted SharePoint Search or Restricted Content Discovery) with an end date.

## 5. Security and compliance (Must)
- DLP and insider-risk policies are reviewed for Copilot locations and content.
- Audit logging is enabled and Copilot interactions are searchable by the security team.
- Data protection impact assessment (DPIA) or equivalent is signed off; the works council has been informed where required.
- A short acceptable-use statement exists (what may be pasted into prompts, how to verify output).

## 6. Agents and extensions (Should)
- Policy for who may create agents and which connectors are allowed is defined.
- Inventory of existing Copilot Studio agents and plugins exists, with owners.
- Web grounding and third-party plugin settings are decided per group.

## 7. Support and operations (Must)
- Service desk has a Copilot knowledge article and routing category.
- Escalation path to the Copilot product owner and to security is documented (see the incident runbook).
- Feedback channel exists (Teams channel or form) and is monitored daily during the pilot.

## 8. Training and communication (Must)
- Launch message, manager briefing and a 30-minute starter session are ready.
- Champions are named: at least one per 30 pilot users.
- A prompt starter list for each target scenario is published.

## Go/no-go summary table
| Area | Owner | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Business case | Sponsor | | |
| Licensing | IT | | |
| Identity | Security | | |
| Data | Data owner | | |
| Security and compliance | CISO/DPO | | |
| Support | Service desk | | |
| Training and comms | Adoption lead | | |

## Example decision
"Wave 1 (60 sales and finance users) is a go. Data readiness is Amber: two finance sites still use Everyone except external users. Owner: site owners, due before day 1; Restricted Content Discovery is enabled on those two sites until fixed."

## Common mistakes
- Treating licenses as the only prerequisite. Permissions hygiene decides what Copilot can surface.
- Skipping the baseline: without a time-per-task baseline you cannot prove value later.
- Rolling out to executives first without a verified permission model; they typically have the broadest access.

title: Copilot pilot evaluation scorecard with metrics and decision gates
summary: A ready-to-use scorecard to evaluate a Microsoft 365 Copilot pilot: adoption, time savings, quality, risk and cost metrics, with thresholds and a scale, adjust, stop decision rule.
body:
# Copilot pilot evaluation scorecard with metrics and decision gates

A pilot without predefined metrics ends in opinions. This scorecard fixes what you measure, where the data comes from, and what result leads to scale, adjust or stop. Agree the thresholds before the pilot starts and sign them off with the sponsor.

## Pilot design (set before day 1)
- Duration: 8 to 12 weeks, with a measured baseline in the two weeks before.
- Cohort: 50 to 150 users from at least three roles; add a comparison group of 20 to 30 non-licensed users in similar roles if you can.
- Cadence: weekly check-in with champions, survey at weeks 2, 6 and end.

## Scorecard
| Dimension | Metric | Source | Target (example) | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Adoption | Active users in last 28 days / licensed users | Copilot usage report in the Microsoft 365 admin center | 70 percent or more | |
| Adoption | Users with 3 or more active days per week | Copilot Dashboard / usage data | 50 percent | |
| Breadth | Apps used per user (Teams, Outlook, Word, Excel...) | Usage report | 3 or more | |
| Productivity | Median minutes saved per scenario | Task-based time study | 20 percent less time | |
| Productivity | Self-reported hours saved per week | Survey | 1.5 hours or more | |
| Quality | Share of outputs used with minor or no edits | Survey sample, 20 outputs per role | 60 percent | |
| Quality | Factual errors found per 20 reviewed outputs | Reviewer log | 2 or fewer | |
| Satisfaction | Net promoter style score (question 0-10, result -100 to 100) | Survey | 40 or more | |
| Risk | Oversharing or data exposure incidents | Security tickets | 0 high severity | |
| Risk | Policy violations in prompts | DLP / audit review | Trend down | |
| Cost | License cost per active user | Finance + usage data | Below value of time saved | |

## Time study method (keep it simple)
1. Pick 3 scenarios per role, for example "summarize a 60-minute meeting and send actions".
2. Measure 5 to 10 executions per user without Copilot (baseline) and with Copilot.
3. Record time to an acceptable result, not just time to first draft.
4. Use the median, not the mean, to reduce outlier impact.
5. Convert minutes to hours per month using the real frequency of the task, not the best case.

## Value calculation example
- 90 active users, 2.0 hours saved per week each, 46 working weeks: 8,280 hours.
- Apply a realization factor of 50 percent (not all saved time becomes productive time): 4,140 hours.
- Multiply by a loaded hourly cost and compare with license plus enablement cost.
- Report the range (pessimistic, expected) rather than one number.

## Decision gates
| Outcome | Rule |
|---|---|
| Scale | Adoption target met, at least two productivity metrics met, no high-severity risk, satisfaction at or above target |
| Adjust | Adoption between 40 and 70 percent or quality below target: extend four weeks with targeted training, new scenarios or role changes |
| Stop or reshape | Adoption below 40 percent after enablement, or any unresolved high-severity data exposure |

## Segment the results
Always split by role and by champion-supported versus unsupported users. A flat average hides that, for example, Sales loves it and Finance does not use it. Decide wave 2 per segment.

## Qualitative evidence
- Collect five concrete stories: task, prompt, result, minutes saved.
- Collect five failures: task, what went wrong, whether data access, prompt quality or model limitation caused it.
- Quote them in the final report; executives remember examples more than percentages.

## Final report outline (two pages)
1. Decision requested and recommendation
2. Scorecard with results against targets
3. Value estimate (range) and cost
4. Risks, incidents and mitigations
5. Segment findings and wave 2 plan
6. Open items and owners

## Common mistakes
- Using license assignment as the adoption metric. Count active users.
- Measuring only enthusiasm. Pair survey data with usage and task data.
- Not capturing the baseline, then arguing about savings for months.
- Letting champions skew the sample; include sceptics deliberately.

title: Content readiness check for Microsoft 365 Copilot: SharePoint and OneDrive permissions, labels and lifecycle
summary: A practical readiness assessment of content, permissions, labels and lifecycle across SharePoint and OneDrive, with scoring, evidence to collect and a remediation priority order.
body:
# Data readiness check before enabling Copilot in SharePoint and OneDrive

Copilot only surfaces what a user can already open, but it makes everything that user can open easy to find. Poor permissions and stale content therefore become visible fast. This check scores your content estate on five dimensions and gives a remediation order.

## Scope
- All SharePoint sites and Teams-connected sites, with priority on the top 100 by activity and the 100 most sensitive.
- OneDrive accounts of the pilot group and of leadership.
- Exchange mailboxes and Teams chats are out of scope for this checklist, but their permissions (delegates, shared mailboxes) need a separate look.

## Scoring (0 = poor, 1 = partial, 2 = good)
| # | Dimension | Question | Score |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Permissions | Are broad principals (Everyone except external users, large all-staff groups) absent from sensitive sites? | |
| 2 | Sharing | Are Anyone links disabled or limited, and do expiry settings exist for guest and company-wide links? | |
| 3 | Labels | Do sensitive files carry a sensitivity label, by default or by auto-labeling? | |
| 4 | Lifecycle | Is every site owned (two owners) and is there a policy for inactive sites? | |
| 5 | Quality | Is outdated, duplicated and draft content marked, archived or removed from search scope? | |

Total 0 to 10. Interpretation: 0-4 not ready (fix first), 5-7 ready for a small controlled pilot with guardrails, 8-10 ready for broader rollout.

## Evidence to collect per dimension
### Permissions
- List of sites with Everyone or Everyone except external users, with owner and sensitivity.
- Sites with more than N unique permission scopes (N depends on your size, start with 50).
- Count of guests with access to confidential sites.

### Sharing
- Tenant and site sharing settings; number of Anyone, People in your organization and Specific people links by site.
- Files shared with external recipients in the last 90 days.

### Labels
- Percentage of files with a label on the top 50 sensitive sites.
- Labeling policies and whether Copilot-relevant label rights (for example EXTRACT in encrypted labels) are understood by the team.

### Lifecycle
- Sites without an owner or with one owner.
- Sites with no activity in 12 months.
- Retention and deletion policies in place.

### Quality
- Libraries with the same document in many versions or copies.
- "Old", "backup", "final_v7" folders in team sites.
- Authoritative sources per topic (policies, price lists, templates) identified.

## Remediation order (highest return first)
1. Remove Everyone except external users from sensitive sites and replace with specific security groups.
2. Set sensitivity labels with default labeling on confidential sites; start auto-labeling for obvious patterns (national IDs, payment data) in simulation mode.
3. Assign owners to ownerless sites; require two owners going forward.
4. Restrict or review sharing: disable Anyone links, set link expiry, review external sharing on the top sites.
5. Archive inactive sites and move stale material out of active libraries.
6. Create authoritative-source sites (policy hub, templates hub) and mark them as the preferred grounding sources for agents.

## Temporary guardrails while remediating
- Restricted SharePoint Search can limit organization-wide search to an allow-list of sites, but it is meant as a short-term measure; set an end date.
- Restricted Content Discovery can hide individual sites from Copilot and search without changing permissions, useful for sensitive sites you cannot fix immediately.
- Record each guardrail with owner, reason and review date in the readiness tracker.

## Example output
"Readiness score 6 of 10. Weakest area: permissions (0). Action: 14 sites shared with Everyone except external users; 9 fixed in week 1, 5 hidden with Restricted Content Discovery until site owners confirm. Pilot starts after week 2 with HR and Legal sites excluded."

## Common mistakes
- Believing sensitivity labels are optional because "Copilot respects permissions". Labels are the second safety net when permissions are wrong.
- Fixing sites one by one without ownership; the problem returns within months.
- Running the scan once. Re-scan monthly and before each wave.
- Cleaning content so aggressively that useful historical knowledge is deleted. Archive first, delete later.

title: SharePoint oversharing review runbook with owner attestation
summary: Step-by-step runbook to find, triage and fix oversharing on SharePoint sites, with severity levels, owner attestation wording, SLAs and an evidence log for audits.
body:
# SharePoint oversharing review runbook with owner attestation

Oversharing means content is accessible to more people than the business intends. It is the most common reason Copilot and search surface surprising results. This runbook turns the cleanup into a repeatable process with owners, SLAs and evidence.

## Roles
- Process owner: head of collaboration or IT governance lead.
- Reviewers: SharePoint administrators.
- Site owners: attest and fix.
- Data protection / security: approve exceptions and handle severity 1 items.

## Step 1: Collect data (week 0)
Gather these reports for the whole tenant:
- Sites with Everyone or Everyone except external users in any permission scope.
- Sharing links by type (Anyone, organization-wide, specific people) per site.
- Sites with guests, and the number of guests.
- Sites with the most unique permission scopes.
- Sensitivity labels applied to files and sites.
Sources: SharePoint Advanced Management data access governance reports, PnP PowerShell or Graph exports, Purview data security posture reports for AI, and the SharePoint admin center active sites list.

## Step 2: Score and triage (week 1)
| Severity | Definition | Example | SLA |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 Critical | Confidential or regulated content exposed to Everyone, Anyone links on confidential files, or external access to restricted data | HR case files readable by all staff | Contain within 1 working day |
| 2 High | Broad group access to internal-only sensitive content | Finance site open to all employees | Fix within 5 working days |
| 3 Medium | Excess access without sensitive content | Project site with former members | Fix within 20 working days |
| 4 Low | Hygiene issues | Empty groups, unused links | Next review cycle |

Sort by severity, then by number of exposed users, then by content volume.

## Step 3: Contain (start immediately for severity 1; severity 2 within its SLA)
- Remove the broad principal or the link; if the owner cannot respond, use a temporary guardrail such as Restricted Content Discovery on the site, or restrict access to site owners.
- Record who made the change, when and why.
- Notify the owner and, for severity 1, security and data protection.

## Step 4: Owner attestation
Send each site owner a request with the data and a clear choice. Suggested wording:

"Subject: Action needed by DATE: access review for SITE NAME
Our review found that this site is accessible to: LIST. Please confirm for each group or link whether the access is still needed for business reasons. Reply with Keep (with the reason), Remove, or Replace with a smaller group. If we do not hear back by DATE, we will send one reminder and inform your manager. If there is still no reply by the reminder deadline, we will restrict access to owners and members you list and hide the site from search and Copilot until you confirm. Contact: ADDRESS."

Send one reminder and inform the owner's manager at the first deadline; auto-restrict if there is still no answer at the reminder deadline.

## Step 5: Fix permanently
- Replace Everyone and broad groups with specific security or Microsoft 365 groups.
- Move to group-based access: members via Microsoft 365 group, owners as named people.
- Apply sensitivity labels to the site (container label) and default labels to libraries.
- Set expiration for guest and organization links; turn off Anyone links for sensitive sites.
- For libraries with unique permissions, restore inheritance where possible.

## Step 6: Verify
- Re-run the same reports and compare counts with step 1.
- Test with a non-member account: search for known sensitive terms and confirm no results.
- Check Copilot responses for two test prompts that would have exposed the content.

## Step 7: Evidence log
Keep one row per site: Site URL, severity, finding, owner, date found, action, date fixed, verified by, exception approved by, review date. This table is what an auditor will ask for.

## Metrics for the monthly report
- Number of sites with Everyone except external users, trend.
- Median days from finding to fix by severity.
- Percentage of sites with two owners.
- Percentage of confidential sites carrying a label.
- Number of active exceptions and how many are overdue for review.

## Common mistakes
- Treating the cleanup as a project. It needs to be a monthly process, because new sites and links appear every day.
- Contacting site owners with raw reports and no recommended action; response rates drop.
- Removing access without notice, which creates helpdesk spikes and resistance.
- Forgetting OneDrive: shared folders in personal OneDrives are a large unreviewed surface.

title: Prompt review rubric for shared team prompt libraries
summary: A 10-point scoring rubric and review workflow for approving prompts into a shared library: clarity, context, output format, data safety, testing and ownership, with examples.
body:
# Prompt review rubric for shared team prompt libraries

A shared prompt library is only useful if the prompts are good, safe and maintained. Use this rubric to review every prompt before it is published, and again at least twice a year.

## Review workflow
1. Author submits the prompt with the template below.
2. Reviewer (a champion or domain expert) scores it against the rubric within three working days.
3. Prompts with 16 points or more and no zero in the safety criteria are published; 12 to 15 are returned with comments; below 12 are rejected.
4. The owner re-tests after major product or model changes and on a fixed review date.

## Submission template
- Title and one-sentence purpose
- Target role and use case
- Application (Copilot Chat, Word, Teams, Outlook, agent)
- The prompt text with placeholders in square brackets
- Required inputs and where the data comes from
- Example output (sanitized)
- Known limits and what to verify
- Owner, version, review date

## Rubric (0 = missing, 1 = partial, 2 = strong)
| # | Criterion | What strong looks like |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Goal clarity | One clear task, stated as an action with a verifiable result |
| 2 | Role and audience | States who the output is for and the tone |
| 3 | Context | Supplies the facts, files or sources the model should use, and says to ignore others |
| 4 | Constraints | Length, structure, do and do-not rules are explicit |
| 5 | Output format | Defines the shape: table, bullets, email, with headings or columns named |
| 6 | Grounding and verification | Asks for sources or references to files and tells the model to say when information is missing |
| 7 | Data safety | No customer data, secrets or personal data embedded; placeholders are used |
| 8 | Reusability | Placeholders are obvious; works for next quarter without edits |
| 9 | Testing evidence | Tested on at least three real inputs with the results noted |
| 10 | Ownership | Named owner, version and review date |

Safety criteria: items 6 and 7. A zero in either blocks publication.

## Example: before and after
Before: "Summarize this meeting."

After: "You are the meeting owner's assistant. Summarize [meeting name] for the project steering group. Use only the meeting transcript and chat. Output: 1) five bullet decisions, 2) a table of actions with owner and due date, 3) open questions. If an owner or date was not stated, write 'not stated'. Keep it under 250 words."

Scoring the before: goal 1, role 0, context 0, constraints 0, format 0, grounding 0, data safety 2, reusability 1, testing 0, ownership 0 = 4 of 20, rejected. Scoring the after: goal 2, role 1, context 2, constraints 2, format 2, grounding 2, data safety 2, reusability 1, testing 0, ownership 0 = 14 of 20, returned with comments until test evidence, an owner and a review date are added.

## Typical findings and fixes
| Finding | Fix |
|---|---|
| Vague verbs ("improve", "look at") | Use specific verbs: summarize, compare, extract, rewrite |
| No output format | Add a table or heading structure |
| Hidden assumptions | Say which files or time range the model should use |
| Customer names in the prompt | Replace with placeholders |
| Prompt asks for legal or medical conclusions | Reframe as a draft for expert review and add a verification line |
| Prompt too long to maintain | Split into steps (prompt chain) or move stable instructions into an agent |

## Library hygiene
- Tag each prompt by role, task and application.
- Show usage count and last review date; archive prompts unused for 6 months.
- Keep a change log: what changed, why, who approved.
- Collect thumbs up/down and comments; a prompt with repeated poor feedback goes back to review.

## Common mistakes
- Publishing prompts that worked once. Require three tests on different inputs.
- Optimizing for length instead of clarity. Short and specific beats long and vague.
- Not telling the model what to do when information is missing, which invites made-up details.
- No owner, so nobody updates the prompt when templates, policies or products change.

title: Agent governance decision matrix for Copilot Studio and declarative agents
summary: A risk-tiering matrix that decides who may build, share and publish agents, which data and connectors are allowed per tier, and which approvals, tests and monitoring each tier requires.
body:
# Agent governance decision matrix for Copilot Studio and declarative agents

Agents multiply quickly: personal helpers, team assistants, autonomous flows. Without tiers, you either block everything or lose control. This matrix classifies every agent by risk and attaches proportionate requirements.

## Step 1: Classify the agent
Answer five questions. Take the highest tier any answer produces.

| Question | Tier 1 (Personal) | Tier 2 (Team) | Tier 3 (Organization) | Tier 4 (Regulated or external) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Who can use it? | Creator only | One team (up to about 50) | Whole company or large groups | Customers, partners or the public |
| What data does it use? | Creator's own files | Team site content, non-confidential | Internal data incl. confidential via connectors | Personal data, financial, health, legal, trade secrets |
| What can it do? | Answer and draft | Answer, draft, create items | Send messages, update records, call APIs | Make or trigger decisions, payments, customer-facing actions |
| Is it autonomous? | No (user prompts) | Triggered by user | Triggered by events or schedule | Runs without human review |
| What is the failure impact? | Annoyance | Rework | Wrong data to many people, compliance issue | Legal, financial or safety impact |

## Step 2: Apply the requirements for the tier
| Requirement | Tier 1 | Tier 2 | Tier 3 | Tier 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Who may build | Any licensed user | Trained makers | Certified makers or IT | IT with business owner and security |
| Environment | Personal or default | Team environment | Dedicated production environment | Dedicated environment with managed solution and ALM |
| Approval | None, registered automatically | Team lead | Business owner plus IT review | Business owner, security, data protection, legal |
| Knowledge sources | Own content | Approved team sites | Approved sources, labels reviewed | Curated sources only, labels enforced |
| Connectors and actions | Standard only | Standard plus approved premium | Allow-list, data policies applied | Allow-list, no custom connectors without review |
| Sharing | Not shared | Named team group | Named groups, no everyone-sharing | Controlled release rings |
| Testing | Creator | Test set of 10 prompts | 30+ prompts including adversarial and permission tests | Full test plan, red-team session, sign-off |
| Human-in-the-loop | Always | Always for writes | For sensitive actions | Required for decisions |
| Logging and monitoring | Platform default | Platform default | Transcripts and analytics reviewed monthly | Alerts, audit review weekly, incident contact on call |
| Review cycle | None | Yearly | Quarterly | Quarterly plus after any change |
| Retirement | Auto-expire after 180 days inactive | Owner confirms yearly | Owner confirms quarterly | Formal decommission plan |

## Step 3: Check identity and ownership
- Every agent has a named owner and a backup owner; ownerless agents are suspended after 30 days.
- Agents that act autonomously have their own identity (not a person's), with least-privilege access and a sponsor.
- Registry entry exists with: name, owner, tier, purpose, data sources, connectors, audience, last review date.

## Step 4: Decide on the request
| Situation | Decision |
|---|---|
| Tier fits and all requirements are met | Approve |
| One requirement missing but low risk | Approve with condition and due date |
| Tier 3 or 4 request without a business owner | Reject until owner is named |
| Agent uses a data source with unresolved oversharing | Hold until the source is cleaned or excluded |
| Agent can write to external systems without human review | Escalate to security |

## Example
Request: "HR onboarding agent answering policy questions for all new hires, reading the HR policy site, creating a ticket in the service tool."
- Audience: organization-wide (Tier 3). Data: HR policies, not personal data (Tier 2). Action: creates a ticket (Tier 3).
- Result: Tier 3. Requirements: business owner (HR lead), IT review, approved connector for the ticket tool, 30-prompt test set, monthly transcript review.
- Condition: policy site must be the single authoritative source; two owners assigned.

## Monitoring signals that trigger re-tiering
- Audience grows beyond the approved group.
- New connector or knowledge source is added.
- Agent starts performing write actions.
- Usage jumps tenfold or the error rate climbs.

## Common mistakes
- Tiering by the maker's intent instead of the audience and the data.
- Letting agents run under the creator's personal credentials after the creator leaves.
- Approving an agent once and never looking again; sources and permissions change.
- Allowing everyone-sharing by default for convenience.

title: Change communication plan and message templates for a Copilot launch
summary: A phased communication plan with audiences, channels, timing and copy-ready message templates for announcing, onboarding and sustaining a Microsoft 365 Copilot rollout.
body:
# Change communication plan and message templates for a Copilot launch

People do not adopt a tool because it exists. They adopt it when they know why it matters for their work, what is allowed, how to start and where to get help. This plan structures the messages across the rollout.

## Audiences and what they need
| Audience | Concern | Message focus |
|---|---|---|
| Executives | Value, risk, cost | Business outcomes, guardrails, how success is measured |
| Managers | Team performance, fairness | How to set expectations, how to coach, what to measure |
| Pilot users | Time, quality | Use cases for their role, quick wins, how to give feedback |
| Champions | Credibility | Talking points, escalation path, early access to updates |
| Works council / data protection | Privacy, monitoring | What data is processed, what is not measured per person |
| Service desk | Ticket load | Known issues, routing, FAQ |
| Everyone else | Fear of being replaced, fairness | What is coming, when, and how they will be supported |

## Timeline
| When | Activity | Channel | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| T-5 weeks | Works council and data protection briefing | Meeting | Project lead |
| T-4 weeks | Sponsor announcement, intent and principles | Email plus leadership meeting | Sponsor |
| T-2 weeks | Manager briefing kit | Manager call | Adoption lead |
| T-1 week | Pilot user invitation and starter session booking | Email | Adoption lead |
| Day 1 | Welcome message with three first tasks | Teams and email | Champions |
| Weeks 1-4 | Weekly tip, weekly office hours | Teams channel | Champions |
| Week 4 | Pulse survey and first results | Survey | Adoption lead |
| End of pilot | Results and next wave decision | Email and town hall | Sponsor |

## Message templates
### 1. Sponsor announcement
Subject: Why we are starting with Microsoft 365 Copilot

"Over the next weeks, a first group of colleagues will try Microsoft 365 Copilot in their daily work. Our goal is simple: spend less time on routine writing, searching and summarizing so that we have more time for customers and quality. This is a pilot. We will measure time saved and quality, and we will decide together how to continue. Three principles: you stay responsible for what you send, we protect company and customer data, and nobody is evaluated by how often they use Copilot. Questions go to QUESTION CHANNEL."

### 2. Manager briefing
"Your team member(s) will receive Copilot on DATE. Please: 1) discuss two use cases for your team in the next team meeting, 2) free 30 minutes for the starter session, 3) ask for examples at the next one-to-one, 4) do not set usage targets; focus on outcomes. Attached: five-slide FAQ and the acceptable-use summary."

### 3. Welcome message (day 1)
"Welcome to the pilot. Try these three tasks today: 1) ask Copilot to summarize your last meeting and list actions, 2) draft a reply to an email thread in Outlook, 3) ask for a one-page summary of a document you know well and check it against the source. Rules of thumb: be specific, give context, always verify facts, never paste confidential customer data into a prompt. Help: CHANNEL, office hours Tuesday 12:00."

### 4. Weekly tip
"Tip of the week: When Copilot's answer is too generic, add three things: who the audience is, what format you need and which file or meeting to use. Example: 'Write a status update for the steering group using the project plan document, five bullets, neutral tone.' Share your best prompt in the channel."

### 5. Service desk note
"Copilot questions: ask for the user's app (Teams, Outlook, Word), the exact prompt and the time. Known issues: LIST. Do not troubleshoot data exposure; escalate to security immediately using the incident category 'Copilot data exposure'."

### 6. Results message
"After WEEKS weeks, ACTIVE percent of pilot users used Copilot at least weekly. Median time for meeting summaries dropped from X to Y minutes. We also found limits: Z. Next step: DECISION. Thank you to our champions."

## Handling common objections
| Objection | Response |
|---|---|
| "It will replace my job" | State the intent plainly: the goal is to remove routine work; commit to what the company will and will not do with the time saved |
| "I do not trust the output" | Agree: verification is part of the process; show the verification habit |
| "Is the company reading my prompts?" | Explain data handling, who can see audit logs and the rules agreed with the works council |
| "I have no time to learn it" | Offer 30-minute role-specific sessions and ready-made prompts |

## Feedback loop
- Monitor the feedback channel daily in the first two weeks; answer within one working day.
- Publish a "you said, we did" note every two weeks.
- Adjust training based on the top three questions.

## Common mistakes
- One big announcement and silence afterwards. Sustain with weekly small messages.
- Hype-based wording. Use specific, modest claims and real examples.
- Forgetting managers: employees follow their manager's signals.
- Measuring individuals' usage in a way that creates fear; report at team or segment level only.

title: Copilot incident response runbook for data exposure and harmful output
summary: A runbook with severity levels, first-hour actions, evidence to collect, containment options, notification decisions and a post-incident review template for Copilot-related incidents.
body:
# Copilot incident response runbook for data exposure and harmful output

Copilot incidents are usually one of five types: a user saw content they should not have (oversharing), sensitive data was entered or leaked via a prompt, an agent took an unintended action, or the output was harmful, biased or wrong in a way that caused damage. This runbook gives the service desk, security and the Copilot owner a shared playbook.

## Incident types
| Type | Example | Typical root cause |
|---|---|---|
| A. Data exposure | Employee asks about salaries and receives results from an HR file | Excess permissions, no label, site not restricted |
| B. Prompt data leakage | Customer data pasted into a prompt or sent to an unapproved plugin | Missing training, permissive plugin policy |
| C. Agent misaction | Agent emails a distribution list or changes a record unintentionally | Missing human approval, broad connector rights |
| D. Harmful or incorrect output | Wrong figure sent to a customer, offensive content | Unverified output, poor grounding |
| E. Prompt injection | Document or email contains hidden instructions that change the answer | Untrusted content in grounding data |

## Severity
| Level | Definition | Response target |
|---|---|---|
| Sev 1 | Regulated or highly confidential data exposed to unauthorized people, or autonomous action with material impact | Start now, containment within 1 hour |
| Sev 2 | Internal sensitive data exposed to a limited group, or customer-facing error | Containment within 4 hours |
| Sev 3 | Low-impact exposure, single user, no sensitive data | Within 2 working days |

## First hour checklist (Sev 1 and 2)
1. Open an incident ticket with category Copilot data exposure; assign an incident lead.
2. Record in the ticket: reporter, time, user, application and which files or sources were cited. Keep the prompt text, the response and screenshots only in the restricted case folder and link to them, so that the ticket does not spread the sensitive content.
3. Do not ask other users to repeat the prompt; avoid spreading the sensitive content further.
4. Identify the source file or site from the citations in the response.
5. Check who has access to the source (site permissions, sharing links, labels).
6. Contain: remove the broad permission or link, or hide the site from Copilot and search with a restriction setting, or unpublish or disable the agent. Pick the least disruptive step that stops the exposure.
7. Confirm containment by testing with a non-privileged test account.
8. Notify security and the data protection officer; for Sev 1 notify the executive sponsor.

## Evidence to collect
- Copilot interaction records from the audit log (user, time, resources accessed).
- Permission history for the source (who gained access and when).
- Sign-in and device context of the affected user.
- Label and DLP policy match results for the content.
- For agents: run history, connector calls and the identity used.
Keep the evidence read-only in a case folder with restricted access.

## Notification decisions
| Question | If yes |
|---|---|
| Was personal data accessed by someone without a business need? | Involve the DPO; assess the legal notification duty and deadlines of your jurisdiction |
| Was customer or partner data exposed? | Check contractual notification clauses |
| Did the exposed audience include people outside the company? | Treat as higher severity; involve legal |
| Did a regulator-relevant system act? | Involve compliance |
Document the reasoning even when you decide not to notify.

## Remediation (after containment)
- Fix the root cause (permissions, labels, plugin policy, agent logic), not just the symptom.
- Search for the same pattern elsewhere: other sites with the same group, other agents with the same connector.
- Add a regression test prompt that previously caused the exposure.
- Update training and the acceptable-use text if user behavior was involved.

## Communication
- To the affected user: short, factual, no blame; explain what was done.
- To the exposed content owner: what was visible, to whom, and what changed.
- To leadership (Sev 1 and 2): impact, containment, root cause, next steps within 24 hours.

## Post-incident review (within 5 working days)
1. Timeline: detection, containment, resolution (with timestamps).
2. Impact: who saw what, for how long.
3. Root cause and contributing factors.
4. What worked, what did not.
5. Actions with owner and due date.
6. Metric: time to detect, time to contain.

## Common mistakes
- Replying to the reporter with the sensitive content again.
- Fixing only the one file instead of the permission pattern.
- Skipping the non-privileged retest, so the exposure remains.
- No pre-agreed contacts: the incident starts with a search for the DPO's phone number.

title: Copilot license allocation decision matrix and reclaim policy
summary: A transparent scoring model for who gets a Copilot license in each wave, plus usage thresholds, grace periods and a reclaim process that keeps licenses with active users.
body:
# Copilot license allocation decision matrix and reclaim policy

When licenses are limited or expensive, "first come first served" and "executives first" both waste money. This matrix scores requests on role fit, use case value and readiness. A reclaim policy then moves unused licenses to people who will use them.

## Principles
- Licenses follow work, not seniority.
- Every license has a named use case and a review date.
- Allocation and reclaim rules are published so people see the process as fair.
- Licenses are assigned through a group; the group owner is the Copilot product owner.

## Allocation scoring (maximum 20 points)
| Criterion | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Content-heavy work (writing, summarizing, analysis) share of week | Under 10 percent | 10-25 | 25-40 | 40-60 | Over 60 percent |
| Meeting load (hours per week in Teams meetings) | Under 3 | 3-8 | 8-14 | 14-20 | Over 20 |
| Information search effort (finding documents, emails) | Rare | Occasional | Weekly | Daily | Constant |
| Measurable use case defined and baseline known | No | Idea only | Defined | Baseline measured | Baseline and target agreed |
| Readiness (training done, manager support, clean data for their area) | None | One | Two | Three | All and champion role |

Scoring bands:
- 15-20: assign in the next wave.
- 10-14: waiting list; assign when licenses free up or after readiness actions.
- Under 10: no license now; offer Copilot Chat and training, review again in six months.

## Quick tiering by role family (starting point, adapt locally)
| Role family | Typical value | Starting priority |
|---|---|---|
| Sales, account and customer success | Meeting recaps, proposal drafts, CRM notes | High |
| Project and program management | Status reports, actions, risk summaries | High |
| Finance and controlling | Excel analysis, variance narratives | Medium-high (data readiness decides) |
| Legal, compliance, HR | Drafting and summarizing, with strict review | Medium (higher risk, strong governance needed) |
| IT and engineering | Documentation, support answers | Medium |
| Frontline and shift workers | Limited fit for the full license | Low; use other offerings |

## Request process
1. Employee or manager submits the request form: role, top three tasks, baseline estimate, manager approval.
2. Product owner scores the request within five working days.
3. Approved users receive a license through the group, plus the starter session invite.
4. A 90-day review date is stored with the assignment.

## Reclaim policy
| Signal | Threshold | Action |
|---|---|---|
| No Copilot activity | 30 days | Reminder with tips and support offer |
| No Copilot activity | 60 days | Manager notified, ask for continued need |
| No Copilot activity | 90 days | License removed; user returns to waiting list |
| Long leave or parental leave | Over 60 days | License suspended and returned to pool |
| Role change | On transfer | Re-score for the new role |
| Leaver | Last working day | License removed through offboarding |

Use the Copilot usage report in the Microsoft 365 admin center for activity data. Note that report latency exists; do not reclaim based on a single day's data.

## Fairness and privacy safeguards
- Activity data is used for license management only, not for performance evaluation; state this in writing and agree it with the works council if you have one.
- Report to managers at team level; individual-level data goes only to the product owner for the reclaim process.
- Appeals: a user can ask for review within 14 days of reclaim with a use case.

## Monthly license dashboard (fields)
Total licenses, assigned, active in 28 days, inactive over 30 days, waiting list size, average score of recent approvals, licenses reclaimed this month.

## Example
Sales manager scores 17 (meeting load 4, content 3, search 3, use case 4, readiness 3). Approved for wave 2. After 62 days of no activity she gets the manager notification; she replies that she was on a trip; license stays with a 30-day check.

## Common mistakes
- Assigning licenses by org chart level and then wondering about low usage.
- Reclaiming silently. Always warn first and offer help.
- No waiting list, so unused licenses sit idle while others ask.
- Mixing performance management with license data, which destroys trust.

title: Quarterly Copilot and agent governance review agenda with evidence pack
summary: A recurring 90-minute governance review with agenda, standing metrics, decision log, evidence checklist and escalation rules for Microsoft 365 Copilot and agents.
body:
# Quarterly Copilot and agent governance review agenda with evidence pack

Governance is not a policy document, it is a recurring decision process with evidence. This quarterly review keeps Copilot and agent use aligned with risk appetite, and produces an audit trail.

## Participants
- Chair: Copilot product owner or head of collaboration.
- Security lead, data protection officer, compliance or risk representative.
- IT operations (Microsoft 365 admin, Power Platform admin).
- Business sponsor and two business representatives (rotating).
- Optional: works council representative, legal.

## Preparation (one week before)
The product owner circulates the evidence pack (below). Participants submit questions in advance. Items without evidence are marked as gaps.

## Agenda (90 minutes)
| Time | Topic | Output |
|---|---|---|
| 0-10 | Review of last quarter's actions | Closed, open, overdue |
| 10-25 | Usage and value: adoption, license use, outcomes | Decision: reallocate, expand, pause |
| 25-45 | Risk and incidents: data exposure, policy violations, near misses | Decision: new controls, retests |
| 45-65 | Agents: inventory, new requests, ownerless or inactive agents | Decision: approve, suspend, retire |
| 65-75 | Data readiness: oversharing trend, label coverage, guest access | Decision: remediation priorities |
| 75-85 | Change radar: new Microsoft features, policy changes, regulatory updates | Decision: adopt, delay, block |
| 85-90 | Decisions and owners recap | Decision log updated |

## Standing metrics
### Adoption and value
- Licensed vs active users (28 days), by department.
- Top five scenarios and measured time saved.
- Cost per active user.

### Risk and compliance
- Copilot-related incidents by severity and time to contain.
- Number of sites shared with Everyone except external users, trend.
- Percentage of confidential sites with a container label.
- DLP and label policy matches involving Copilot interactions.
- Active exceptions and overdue exception reviews.

### Agents
- Agents by tier, owner present yes or no, last review date.
- New agents in quarter and agents retired.
- Agents with write actions or external connectors.
- Ownerless agents (target: zero).

### Operations
- Open Copilot support tickets and median resolution time.
- Training completion among licensed users.

## Evidence pack checklist
- [ ] Usage report export (date range stated)
- [ ] License assignment list with group membership
- [ ] Incident log with root causes
- [ ] Oversharing report before and after
- [ ] Agent registry export with tier and owner
- [ ] Policy configuration snapshot: sharing, plugins, web grounding, data policies
- [ ] Audit log search for Copilot activity: sample reviewed
- [ ] Decision log of the last meeting with action status
- [ ] Message Center and roadmap items affecting Copilot

## Decision log format
| ID | Date | Decision | Rationale | Owner | Due | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| G-2026-Q4-01 | | Disable web grounding for the legal group | Unclear sources for legal work | Security lead | | Open |

## Escalation rules
- Any Sev 1 incident: sponsor and CISO informed within 24 hours, not on the quarterly cycle.
- Two consecutive quarters with the same unresolved high risk: escalate to the executive committee.
- A request to relax a control needs a written risk acceptance signed by the business owner.

## Annual additions (once per year)
- Re-run the risk assessment and update the agent tier matrix.
- Review the acceptable-use text and training content.
- Test the incident runbook with a tabletop exercise.
- Revalidate vendor and data-processing documentation.

## Common mistakes
- Discussing opinions instead of numbers; always bring the pack.
- No decision log, so the same topics return every quarter.
- Excluding business representatives and ending with controls nobody wants to follow.
- Treating Microsoft feature changes as background noise; new defaults can change your risk profile overnight.
